en.title: Information Systems: the whole course
en.short: What Information Systems covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
An information system is the organised combination of people, business processes, data and technology that an organisation uses to collect, store and share information. The technology is only one part. A clinic’s patient records, a bank’s transfer system and a trader’s stock book are all information systems, whether or not a computer is involved.

The subject sits between computing and management. You learn how systems are built, but also why an organisation needs them, who uses them and what they cost. That is why the course mixes technical topics such as databases and networks with business topics such as processes, strategy and project management.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degrees differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook for the rules that apply to your intake.

In Nigeria, a BSc usually runs for four years, from 100 to 400 level. The National Universities Commission (NUC) sets minimum standards through its Core Curriculum and Minimum Academic Standards (CCMAS), which replaced the older Benchmark Minimum Academic Standards (BMAS). Many programmes include industrial training under SIWES, often in the long vacations. Polytechnics award the ND and HND under NBTE standards, with more practical work.

In England a first degree usually takes three years. In Ghana and Kenya it often takes four. A master’s degree usually takes one to two years and ends with a dissertation or a large project.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The early topics build foundations. You start with information systems in organisations and business processes, then computer hardware and software, data representation and number systems, and networks and the internet. Programming fundamentals and spreadsheets come next, because you need to handle data yourself. Then databases and web technologies give you the two skills most systems depend on.

The core stage turns these foundations into professional practice. Systems analysis and design and requirements engineering teach you to find out what a system must do. Data modelling and database design show how to structure the data. Business process management, enterprise systems and ERP, and project management cover how work is organised. Strategy and governance, e-commerce, business intelligence, data warehousing and data mining, security and risk, cloud infrastructure, human-computer interaction, and professional practice, ethics and law widen the view. Emerging technologies closes the stage.

At master’s level the work becomes more analytical: research methods and theory, advanced analytics and machine learning, digital platforms and transformation strategy, and socio-technical design and AI ethics.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the vocabulary early and use it precisely. Terms such as process, requirement, entity, normalisation and governance carry exact meanings in exams and in practice.

Practise the practical parts on a small case. Take one organisation you know, such as a shop or a school office, and model it: draw its processes, list its entities, sketch its database and write a few use cases. Doing this once properly teaches more than reading five chapters.

For the technical topics, work through examples by hand. Normalise a table step by step. Convert numbers between bases. Write and run small programs and spreadsheet formulas. For the management topics, write short answers in full sentences and give an example each time.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often make these mistakes:
Treating information systems as only IT, and forgetting people and processes.
Confusing data, information and knowledge.
Mixing up analysis (what is needed) with design (how it will be built).
Drawing diagrams without a clear key or consistent notation.
Skipping normalisation rules and then wondering why a database misbehaves.
Memorising definitions without an example.
Ignoring the legal and ethical side, especially data protection.
Leaving the project or dissertation late.

keyPoints: An information system is people, processes, data and technology together, not just software.
The course moves from foundations, to core professional practice, to analytical master’s work.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Model one real organisation yourself; it teaches more than reading several chapters.
Keep analysis and design separate, and always attach an example to a definition.
Data protection law and professional ethics are part of the subject, not an afterthought.

en.title: Information systems in organisations
en.short: Data, information and knowledge, the parts of an information system, main system types and their roles.

sections.heading: Data, information, knowledge
sections.text: Data are raw facts that carry no meaning on their own, such as 4,200 or 17 March. Information is data processed into a form that answers a question: sales on 17 March were 4,200 cartons. Knowledge is what a person or organisation understands and can act on: a 4,200-carton day means the warehouse must restock before Friday. The move from data to information to knowledge is often drawn as a pyramid. Each step takes work: sorting, summarising, comparing and interpreting with experience.

sections.heading: Parts of a system
sections.text: An information system is a set of parts that collect, process, store and distribute information, with feedback to keep it on course. The usual five components are hardware, software, data, people and processes, meaning the rules people follow. Some textbooks add networks, or treat them as part of hardware. All five matter: a good database with untrained staff and no procedures still fails.

sections.heading: System types
sections.text: Textbooks group systems by the level they serve. A transaction processing system (TPS) records routine events such as sales and payments, and must be fast and reliable. A management information system (MIS) summarises TPS data into regular reports for managers. A decision support system (DSS) helps with one less structured decision by letting a manager test alternatives, such as what if we raise the price by 5 per cent. An executive information system (EIS) gives senior managers a brief dashboard of key figures. Real systems often mix these roles.

sections.heading: Roles in organisations
sections.text: Systems earn their place by doing several jobs: handling volume and routine, supporting decisions, coordinating people and suppliers, keeping records for law and audit, and sometimes creating advantage. Case: Adaeze runs a food distributor in Enugu. Her TPS records each order. Her MIS prints a weekly sales report by product. Before buying a second van she uses a DSS to compare delivery costs. The owner checks an EIS dashboard each Monday. No single system does all of this well.

keyPoints: Data are raw facts; information is data processed to answer a question; knowledge is understanding that guides action.
An information system has five usual components: hardware, software, data, people and processes.
A TPS records routine transactions and is the main source of data for other systems.
An MIS turns TPS data into regular summary reports for managers.
A DSS supports a single, less structured decision; an EIS gives executives a brief dashboard.
Information systems support efficiency, decisions, coordination, record keeping and sometimes competitive advantage.

en.title: Business processes and value chains
en.short: Process view, process mapping, Porter’s value chain and how information systems support and change processes.

sections.heading: Process view
sections.text:
A business process is a set of linked activities that turns an input into an output of value to a customer. The process view sees an organisation as a system of processes, rather than as separate departments.

It asks what work is done, in what order, by whom, and how well. Processes cross departmental boundaries, so improving one step can expose a delay elsewhere. A process has a trigger, inputs, activities, outputs and a customer.

sections.heading: Mapping processes
sections.text:
Process mapping draws a process as a diagram. A simple map uses start and end, boxes for activities, diamonds for decisions and arrows for flow. A swimlane map adds lanes for each person or department, showing handoffs and waiting.

Map the process as it really runs, not as managers think it runs. Then mark delays, repeated work and errors. Example: Amina’s bakery in Kano takes orders on paper. Its map shows order, stock check, baking, packaging, invoice and payment, and reveals stock is checked twice, once when the order is taken and again before baking.

sections.heading: Value chains
sections.text:
Michael Porter’s value chain describes the activities through which a firm creates value. Primary activities are inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service. Support activities are firm infrastructure, human resource management, technology development and procurement.

The chain includes a margin: value to the customer minus the cost of the activities. A firm can gain advantage by performing an activity better or cheaper than rivals, or by reconfiguring the chain. Information systems can link activities and share data along it.

sections.heading: Systems and context
sections.text:
Information systems support processes by storing data, automating steps, checking rules and connecting people. They also change processes: an online order system may remove a data-entry step and update stock at once.

But a system is not only software. It includes people, data, rules and the organisation around it. The same system can succeed in one firm and fail in another because of culture, skills, incentives and work practices. Understand the process and context before judging the technology.

keyPoints: A business process is a linked set of activities that turns inputs into outputs of value to a customer.
The process view examines how work flows across departments, not just the departmental structure.
Process maps show activities, decisions, flows and handoffs, and help find delays and repeated work.
Porter’s value chain divides activities into primary and support activities and includes a margin.
Information systems can support processes by storing data, automating steps and connecting people, and can also change them.
A system must be understood with its people, rules and organisational context, because the same technology can succeed or fail in different firms.

en.title: Computer hardware and software
en.short: Main hardware parts, operating system functions, and system versus application software.

sections.heading: Hardware components
sections.text: Hardware is the physical parts of a computer. The central processing unit (CPU) executes instructions. Main memory, usually random access memory (RAM), holds active programs and data; it is volatile, so it loses contents when power is off. Secondary storage, such as a solid state drive (SSD) or hard disk drive (HDD), keeps files permanently. Input devices, such as a keyboard or sensor, bring data in. Output devices, such as a screen or printer, present results. A motherboard, the main circuit board, connects the parts.

sections.heading: Operating system
sections.text: An operating system (OS) is system software that manages the computer. It schedules processes, allocates memory, controls input and output, manages files and provides a user interface. It also enforces access rights and lets programs share hardware safely. Examples are Windows, macOS, Linux and Android; the right choice depends on the needed software.

sections.heading: Software types
sections.text: System software runs and controls the computer itself. It includes the OS, device drivers, which let the OS talk to hardware, and utility programs such as backup tools. Application software helps a user do a task, such as a word processor, payroll system or stock control system. Application software depends on system software. The difference is purpose: system software supports the machine; application software supports the user’s work.

sections.heading: Choices in systems
sections.text:
Hardware and software choices affect cost, speed, reliability, security and growth. Too little RAM or storage slows a system and may cause failure under load. Software must match the hardware and OS, and staff must be able to use it. These choices decide what data an information system can capture, store, process and report.

Case: Amina runs a small clinic in Kano. She needs a computer to record visits, print receipts and back up files. She chooses an SSD for speed, enough RAM for the records application, and an OS that supports her software and printer. A cheaper machine that cannot run the software would cost more in lost time.

keyPoints: Hardware includes the CPU, memory, storage, input and output devices, and the motherboard.
RAM is volatile, while secondary storage keeps data when power is off.
An operating system manages processes, memory, files, input and output, access rights and the user interface.
System software runs the computer; application software helps users perform tasks.
Hardware and software choices affect cost, speed, security, compatibility and scalability.
In an information system, these choices determine what data can be captured, stored, processed and reported.

en.title: Data representation and number systems
en.short: Binary, decimal and hexadecimal, storage units, character encoding and simple binary arithmetic.

sections.heading: Why representation matters
sections.text: Computers store and move every item as bits. A bit is one binary digit, 0 or 1. A byte is eight bits. Representation is the agreed rule that gives bits meaning, such as a number, letter, image or instruction. The same byte can mean different things under different rules. Good representation matters for storage size, transmission speed, correct comparison and sorting, and exchange between systems. If two systems use different encodings, text can arrive corrupted.

sections.heading: Number systems
sections.text:
Decimal uses ten digits, 0 to 9, and place values that are powers of 10. Binary uses two digits, 0 and 1, and place values that are powers of 2. Hexadecimal uses sixteen symbols, 0 to 9 and A to F, where A = 10 and F = 15. Hex is compact because one hex digit stands for four bits.

Example: 1011 1100 in binary groups as B and C in hex, so 0xBC = 11 × 16 + 12 = 188. Decimal 13 is 1101 in base 2 because 8 + 4 + 1 = 13.

sections.heading: Storage and encoding
sections.text:
Storage units start with the bit and byte. Multiples vary: SI decimal prefixes use 1000 (1 kB = 1000 bytes), while binary prefixes use 1024 (1 KiB = 1024 bytes). Check which convention a device or specification uses.

Character encoding maps characters to numbers. ASCII defines 128 codes in seven bits. Extended ASCII variants differ. Unicode assigns a code point to almost every character; UTF-8 stores each code point in one to four bytes. Encoding affects file size and whether text displays correctly.

sections.heading: Binary arithmetic
sections.text:
Binary addition works like decimal addition but carries at 2. Add 1011 in base 2 (11) and 0110 in base 2 (6):
  1011
+ 0110
=10001 in base 2
The result is 17. Subtraction borrows 2. 1011 in base 2 − 0110 in base 2 = 0101 in base 2 (5).

keyPoints: One hex digit represents four binary bits.
Decimal 13 = 1101 in base 2 and 0xBC = 188.
1 byte = 8 bits; decimal and binary prefixes differ (1000 versus 1024).
ASCII has 128 seven-bit codes; Unicode with UTF-8 uses one to four bytes per character.
Binary addition carries at 2: 1011 in base 2 + 0110 in base 2 = 10001 in base 2.
Representation rules determine storage size, correct display and reliable exchange.

en.title: Networks and the internet
en.short: LANs, WANs, IP addressing, DNS, HTTP, client-server, and basic cloud services.

sections.heading: Networks and scale
sections.text: A network connects devices so they can exchange data. A local area network (LAN) covers one site, such as a campus or office, and is usually owned by that organisation. A wide area network (WAN) spans cities or countries and often uses links leased from telecom operators. The internet is the global network of networks that uses the TCP/IP protocol suite. Data is broken into packets, and routers forward packets between networks.

sections.heading: IP addresses and DNS
sections.text: An IP address identifies a device interface on a network. IPv4 uses 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers, for example 192.168.1.10. IPv6 uses 128 bits, written in hexadecimal. A subnet mask shows which bits name the network. With mask 255.255.255.0, the example address lies in network 192.168.1.0/24; addresses .1 to .254 are normally usable hosts, while .0 and .255 are reserved. The Domain Name System (DNS) maps names such as example.com to IP addresses using distributed name servers.

sections.heading: Client-server and HTTP
sections.text: The client-server model divides work between a client that asks for a service and a server that provides it. A web browser is a client; a web server stores and returns pages. HTTP is the request-response protocol of the web. A request names a method such as GET or POST and a resource. A response carries a status code, such as 200 for success or 404 for not found, plus headers and often a body. HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS (Transport Layer Security) encryption. HTTP is stateless, so cookies are often used to remember a user between requests.

sections.heading: Internet, web and cloud
sections.text: The internet is the transport platform; the web is one service built on it. Information systems use both to reach users, link organisations and call remote services. Cloud services provide computing resources over a network, usually with pay-as-you-go pricing. Common models are infrastructure as a service (IaaS), platform as a service (PaaS) and software as a service (SaaS). Exact offerings and prices vary by provider and country, so check current official information.

keyPoints: LANs cover a site; WANs span large distances; the internet is a global network of networks using TCP/IP.
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; IPv6 addresses are 128 bits; a subnet mask separates network and host bits.
DNS maps domain names to IP addresses.
HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol; HTTPS adds TLS encryption.
The client-server model separates service requesters from service providers.
Cloud services deliver computing resources over a network, often as IaaS, PaaS or SaaS.

en.title: Programming fundamentals for information systems
en.short: Variables, data types, control flow, functions and input/output for automating business rules.

sections.heading: Building blocks
sections.text: A program in a general-purpose language is a list of instructions a computer follows. A variable is a named storage location whose value can change. A data type says what kind of value a variable holds and which operations are allowed: integer (whole number), float (decimal number), string (text) and Boolean (true or false). In Python-like pseudocode, unit_price = 250 creates an integer variable. Use meaningful names such as unit_price rather than x. A constant is a value not meant to change; by convention its name is in capitals.

sections.heading: Control flow
sections.text: Control flow decides which instructions run and how often. An if statement runs a block only when a condition is true; else gives the alternative. A while loop repeats while a condition holds; a for loop repeats over a known sequence. Comparison operators such as ==, < and >= produce Boolean values. Indentation marks blocks in Python; many other languages use braces. Example: if stock <= reorder_level: print('Reorder').

sections.heading: Functions and I/O
sections.text: A function is a named block that takes inputs (parameters), does one job and may return a value. Functions avoid repetition and make business rules easier to test. Input reads data, often as text, so convert it: quantity = int(input('Quantity: ')). Output displays results with print. A function can combine input, calculation and output.

sections.heading: Automating a rule
sections.text:
Small script for a shop:
def order_total(unit_price, quantity):
    return unit_price * quantity
def reorder_needed(stock, level):
    return stock <= level
unit_price = 250
quantity = 12
stock = 5
level = 10
total = order_total(unit_price, quantity)
print('Total:', total)
print('Reorder:', reorder_needed(stock, level))
Output: Total: 3000 and Reorder: True. The rule is checked automatically, so staff need not compare figures by hand.

keyPoints: A variable is a named storage location with a data type that limits its allowed values and operations.
Control flow uses conditions and loops to choose and repeat instructions.
A function packages a task, takes parameters and may return a result.
Input usually arrives as text, so convert it to int or float before arithmetic.
Small scripts can automate business rules such as reorder checks and order totals.
Use meaningful names and test functions with known values.

en.title: Spreadsheets and business quantitative methods
en.short: Spreadsheet formulas, functions and charts, with percentages, ratios, interest, statistics and probability.

sections.heading: Formulas and functions
sections.text: A formula starts with = and combines cell references, numbers and operators such as + − * / ^. Relative references like A1 change when copied; absolute references like $A$1 stay fixed. Functions are built-in formulas: SUM adds a range, AVERAGE gives the mean, COUNT counts numbers, IF chooses between results, and ROUND sets decimals. A model links formulas so inputs and assumptions produce outputs. Keep inputs separate, label units, and test with known values.

sections.heading: Percentages and ratios
sections.text: To find a percentage of a value, multiply by percentage ÷ 100. Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. A ratio compares quantities, such as 3:2, and scales by multiplying both parts. Ratios can become fractions or percentages for analysis. Example: a price rises from 80 to 100. Change = (100 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = 25%. The new price is 125% of the old.

sections.heading: Interest and charts
sections.text: Simple interest = principal × rate × time, with rate as a decimal. Compound interest adds interest each period: amount = principal × (1 + rate)^n, where n is periods. Example: 100,000 at 10% for 2 years gives simple interest 100,000 × 0.10 × 2 = 20,000. Compound amount = 100,000 × 1.10² = 121,000, so interest is 21,000. Charts show results: column charts compare categories, line charts show trends, and pie charts show parts of a whole. Use the simplest chart that answers the question.

sections.heading: Statistics and probability
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise data. Mean = sum ÷ count. Median is the middle value of sorted data. Mode is the most frequent value. Range = largest − smallest. Standard deviation measures spread. For 4, 6, 8, 10: mean = 28 ÷ 4 = 7, median = 7, range = 6, population standard deviation = √5 ≈ 2.24. Probability is chance from 0 to 1: P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. For a fair die, P(even) = 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5.

keyPoints: Formulas start with = and use cell references; $ fixes a reference when copied.
Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
Simple interest = P × r × t; compound amount = P × (1 + r)^n.
Mean = sum ÷ count; range = largest − smallest.
Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, always between 0 and 1.
Choose charts by purpose: columns compare, lines show trends, pies show parts.

en.title: Introduction to databases
en.short: Relational tables, rows, columns and keys, simple SQL queries, and what a DBMS does.

sections.heading: Tables and the relational model
sections.text: A database is an organised collection of related data. The relational model, set out by E. F. Codd in 1970, stores data in tables, also called relations. A table has columns (fields or attributes) and rows (records or tuples). Each column holds one kind of value, from a set of allowed values called its domain. Each row is one complete record. Row and column order carries no meaning; the values do.

sections.heading: Primary and foreign keys
sections.text:
A primary key is a column, or a few columns together, whose value is unique in every row and never empty. It identifies each row. A foreign key is a column holding a primary key value from another table, which is how tables are linked.

Case: a college in Ibadan keeps Student(StudentID, Name) and Enrolment(StudentID, CourseCode, Mark). StudentID is the primary key of Student. In Enrolment it is part of the primary key and also a foreign key to Student, so the database rejects an enrolment for a student who does not exist.

sections.heading: Simple SQL queries
The role of the DBMS
sections.text: A database management system (DBMS) is the software that stores and retrieves the data, such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle Database or Microsoft SQL Server. It keeps data on disk, answers queries, controls who may read or change what, stops two users overwriting each other, enforces keys, and recovers data after a failure. Because many applications share one copy, the organisation avoids the duplicated, conflicting records that separate files produce.

keyPoints: A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns.
A primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be empty.
A foreign key holds a primary key value from another table and links the two tables.
SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE retrieves rows, and JOIN combines tables on a shared key.
A DBMS stores, retrieves, secures and protects an organisation’s shared data.
SQL is an international standard, but each product adds its own extensions.

en.title: Web technologies and digital presence
en.short: HTML, CSS, the client-server web, forms, content management, digital channels and basic web security.

sections.heading: Pages and style
sections.text: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) gives a web page structure: headings, paragraphs, links and images. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls presentation such as colour, spacing and layout. Keeping structure in HTML and style in CSS makes a site easier to maintain and adapt to phones. HTML is not a programming language; it marks up content.

sections.heading: Client and server
sections.text:
The web uses the client-server model. A browser is the client. It sends an HTTP request to a web server, which returns a response, often HTML, CSS and JavaScript. HTTP is the protocol for these requests. The server may run code to fetch data or check a login.

An HTML form collects input with fields and a submit button. Its action names the server address; its method is usually GET or POST. GET puts data in the URL and suits searches; POST sends data in the request body and suits changes. The server must validate every submission; browser checks alone are not enough.

sections.heading: Managing content
sections.text:
A content management system (CMS) stores content separately from design. Authors edit pages in an admin area, choose a template, and publish. Roles limit who may edit or approve. This suits organisations that update news, products or policies often.

Digital presence is how an organisation appears online: website, search results, social media, email and listings. A consistent name, contact details and message help trust. For example, Ada’s tailoring shop in Lagos uses a CMS site for prices and opening hours, plus social posts for new designs.

sections.heading: Staying safe
sections.text: Basic web security awareness means knowing common risks. HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt traffic between browser and server; users should see it on login and payment pages. Passwords should be stored hashed, not as plain text. Validate and escape all input before display to reduce injection attacks. Keep software updated, use least privilege, and train staff to recognise phishing. These measures support, but do not replace, a full security programme.

keyPoints: HTML structures content and CSS controls presentation.
In the client-server model, a browser sends HTTP requests and a web server returns responses.
GET places form data in the URL; POST sends it in the request body, and the server must validate all input.
A CMS separates content from design and uses roles and templates to manage publishing.
Digital presence covers every online channel where an organisation appears, so consistency matters.
HTTPS encrypts traffic with TLS, and basic awareness includes hashed passwords, input escaping, updates and phishing training.

en.title: Systems analysis and design
en.short: The SDLC, methodologies, feasibility and introductory process and data modelling for design.

sections.heading: The life cycle
sections.text: The systems development life cycle (SDLC) is the organised set of stages for building or changing an information system. A common version runs: planning, analysis, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. Planning sets scope and the business case. Analysis studies the current situation and states what the new system must do. Design states how it will do it. Implementation builds it, testing checks it, deployment releases it, and maintenance corrects and improves it. Stages may overlap and repeat; the SDLC is a map, not a rule that every project follows in one straight line.

sections.heading: Methodologies
sections.text: A methodology is a defined way of organising the work. Waterfall completes each stage before the next and suits stable, well understood requirements. Iterative and incremental methods deliver a system in repeated cycles. Agile methods, such as Scrum, use short iterations and frequent user feedback. Prototyping builds a quick model to clarify requirements. Spiral adds risk analysis to repeated cycles. They differ in sequence, documentation, user involvement and how they treat change. Waterfall controls change tightly; agile expects it.

sections.heading: Feasibility
sections.text: Feasibility analysis asks whether a proposed system is worth and possible to build. Technical feasibility checks whether the technology and skills exist. Economic feasibility compares costs with expected benefits. Operational feasibility asks whether users and processes can accept it. Schedule feasibility asks whether it can be delivered in time. Legal and ethical checks may also apply. A project that fails feasibility should be stopped or reshaped before design.

sections.heading: Analysis to design
sections.text: Analysis produces models of requirements. Process models, such as data flow diagrams, show inputs, processes, stores and outputs. Data models, such as entity relationship diagrams, show entities, attributes and relationships. Design turns these into architecture, screens, reports, process specifications and a logical data schema. A clinic in Kano, Nigeria, uses paper appointment books. Analysis finds long waits and lost records; design proposes Patient and Appointment entities, a booking process and a daily schedule report. Models trace back to requirements.

keyPoints: The SDLC commonly runs from planning and analysis through design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance.
Analysis defines what the system must do; design defines how it will do it.
Waterfall is sequential, while iterative and agile methods repeat work in cycles and expect change.
Feasibility analysis covers technical, economic, operational and schedule concerns before design.
Process models show how work flows, and data models show the things stored and their relationships.
Design decisions should trace back to requirements so that the built system solves the stated problem.

en.title: Requirements engineering and use cases
en.short: Eliciting, specifying, validating and tracing requirements, with use cases and stakeholder conflicts.

sections.heading: Eliciting requirements
sections.text: Requirements engineering is the work of finding, stating, checking and managing what a system must do. Elicitation uses interviews, workshops, observation of real work, document study and prototypes. Stakeholders include users, managers, regulators and IT staff, and their goals often conflict. In a clinic in Kano, nurses want fast check-in, doctors want full patient history, and the accountant wants billing reports. A good analyst records who asked for each requirement and why.

sections.heading: Functional and non-functional
sections.text: Functional requirements say what the system must do, such as book an appointment or print a receipt. Non-functional requirements are quality constraints: response time, security, usability, availability and legal rules. They must be measurable. 'The system must be fast' is weak. 'A search returns results within two seconds for 95 per cent of requests’ can be tested. Missing non-functional requirements often cause a system to be rejected even when its functions work.

sections.heading: Use cases
sections.text: A use case describes one goal an actor pursues with the system. An actor is a person or external system. 'Book an appointment' has the patient as actor. The use case description gives the main flow and alternate flows, such as the chosen slot being taken. A use case diagram shows which actors use which use cases; it does not show sequence. The written description is more useful for design and testing.

sections.heading: Validation and traceability
sections.text: Validation checks that requirements are correct, complete, consistent and testable. Reviews, prototypes and early test cases expose ambiguity. Traceability links each requirement to its source, design, code and tests, often in a traceability matrix. Poor requirements cause project failure through rework, disputes and unused software. If 'fast' is never made measurable, developers guess, testers cannot verify, and the client may refuse the result.

keyPoints: Elicitation uses interviews, workshops, observation and prototypes, and stakeholders often disagree.
Functional requirements state what the system does; non-functional requirements state quality constraints and must be measurable.
A use case is an actor’s goal with a main flow and alternate flows.
Validation checks requirements for correctness, completeness, consistency and testability.
Traceability links each requirement to its source, design, code and tests.
Poor requirements cause rework, disputes and unused systems.

en.title: Data modelling and database design
en.short: Entity-relationship modelling, normalisation to 3NF, relational schemas and SQL for integrity.

sections.heading: Entity-relationship modelling
sections.text:
An entity-relationship (ER) model describes data before tables exist. An entity is a thing we store data about, such as Patient. An attribute is a property of an entity. A relationship links entities; cardinality says how many: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.

In a clinic, a patient makes many visits, and each visit involves one doctor. A many-to-many relationship, such as Student to Course, becomes a separate table.

sections.heading: Normalisation to 3NF
sections.text:
Normalisation reduces redundancy and update anomalies by grouping attributes into tables based on functional dependencies. A functional dependency X -> Y means each X value determines at most one Y value. First normal form (1NF) requires atomic values and no repeating groups. Second normal form (2NF) is 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite key. Third normal form (3NF) is 2NF plus no transitive dependency: non-key attributes depend only on the key.

Example: Visit(VisitID, PatientID, PatientName, DoctorID, DoctorPhone). PatientName depends on PatientID, so move patients out; DoctorPhone depends on DoctorID, so move doctors out. Visit keeps VisitID, PatientID, DoctorID, date.

sections.heading: Relational schema and SQL
sections.text:
The relational schema states each table, its columns, primary key and foreign keys. A primary key is unique and not null. A foreign key references a primary key in another table.

SQL data definition language (DDL) creates and changes structures: CREATE TABLE Patient (PatientID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL); SQL data manipulation language (DML) works with rows: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE. ON DELETE RESTRICT stops a doctor being deleted while visits refer to that doctor.

sections.heading: Integrity and redundancy
sections.text:
Good design supports integrity. Entity integrity means primary keys are unique and not null. Referential integrity means every foreign key matches an existing primary key or is null.

Normalisation reduces duplicated data, so one change is made in one place. This avoids anomalies: if a patient’s name is stored once, changing it cannot leave conflicting copies. Designers sometimes denormalise for speed, but must manage the extra risk.

keyPoints: An ER model identifies entities, attributes, relationships and cardinality before tables are built.
1NF requires atomic values; 2NF removes partial dependencies; 3NF removes transitive dependencies.
A relational schema names tables, columns, primary keys and foreign keys.
SQL DDL defines structures with CREATE and ALTER; SQL DML works with rows using INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE.
Entity integrity keeps primary keys unique and not null; referential integrity keeps foreign keys valid.
Normalisation reduces redundancy and update anomalies, though deliberate denormalisation trades this for speed.

en.title: Business process management
en.short: Process identification, BPMN modelling, improvement, automation and performance measurement.

sections.heading: Identifying processes
sections.text: Business process management (BPM) is a disciplined way to find, model, improve, automate and monitor the processes an organisation uses to deliver value. Process identification decides which processes matter, where each starts and ends, and who owns it. A process architecture groups them, for example core processes that serve customers and support processes such as procurement. Teams prioritise by impact and feasibility, not by enthusiasm alone.

sections.heading: Modelling with BPMN
sections.text: Process modelling makes the current process (as-is) and the intended process (to-be) visible. BPMN, the Business Process Model and Notation, is a standard diagram language with events, activities, gateways, sequence flows, pools and lanes. A gateway shows a decision or parallel split. Pools separate organisations and lanes separate roles. A model should be readable by business staff, not only analysts.

sections.heading: Improvement and automation
sections.text: Improvement removes waste: waiting, duplication, unnecessary checks and handoffs. Automation then uses information systems to execute or support the redesigned process. A workflow or BPMS (business process management system) routes work, applies rules and records status. Robotic process automation (RPA) copies user actions across systems and suits stable, rule-based tasks. Information systems enable change by capturing data once, coordinating work across departments, enforcing business rules and exposing process data for monitoring. Automating a poor process only makes it faster and more consistently wrong.

sections.heading: Measuring performance
sections.text: Evaluate a process with cycle time, throughput, waiting time, defect rate, cost per case and service-level compliance. Cycle time is the elapsed time from start to finish, including waiting. Throughput is completed cases per unit time. Case: at a Lagos retailer, purchase approval has 60 minutes of work and 30 minutes of waiting, so cycle time is 90 minutes. Removing 30 minutes of waiting gives 60 minutes, a 30 ÷ 90 = 33% reduction. If one case is handled at a time, throughput rises from 480 ÷ 90 = 5.3 to 480 ÷ 60 = 8 cases per 8-hour day. Check capacity and demand before promising such gains.

keyPoints: BPM follows a cycle: identify, model, improve, automate and monitor processes.
BPMN uses events, activities, gateways, sequence flows, pools and lanes to model as-is and to-be processes.
Automation should follow redesign; automating a poor process makes its faults faster and more consistent.
Information systems enable process change by capturing data once, coordinating work, enforcing rules and monitoring events.
Cycle time is elapsed time including waiting; throughput is completed cases per unit time.
Use cycle time, throughput, defect rate, cost per case and service-level compliance to evaluate a process.

en.title: Enterprise systems: ERP, CRM and SCM
en.short: ERP, CRM and SCM systems, integration, implementation risks, vendor choice and organisational change.

sections.heading: Enterprise systems
sections.text: An enterprise system is a large software package that supports many parts of an organisation on shared data. Enterprise resource planning (ERP) covers core transactions such as finance, purchasing, inventory, production and payroll. Customer relationship management (CRM) manages sales leads, customer records, service requests and marketing campaigns. Supply chain management (SCM) plans and tracks materials, suppliers, orders and deliveries. Each can be bought as a package and configured, rather than written from scratch.

sections.heading: Integration
sections.text: Integration means making these systems share data and trigger each other’s processes. A single ERP database reduces duplicate entry: when a customer order is entered, stock is reserved and an invoice is raised. CRM and SCM often connect to ERP through middleware, which is software that translates messages and moves data between systems. Master data, the shared records for customers, products and suppliers, must be defined once and governed. Poor integration creates reconciliation work and conflicting reports.

sections.heading: Implementation and vendors
sections.text: Implementation is risky because packages impose their own process logic. Common challenges are unclear requirements, poor data quality, customisation that makes upgrades hard, weak testing and underestimated training. Vendor selection compares fit to processes, total cost of ownership, support, references, integration options and the vendor’s stability. A phased rollout by module or site is common. Contracts should define scope, service levels and exit terms.

sections.heading: Organisational change
sections.text: An enterprise system changes who enters data, who approves actions and how work is measured. Resistance is normal. Success needs visible sponsorship, user involvement, process redesign before configuration, training and communication. Case: Adeyemi Foods, a Nigerian distributor, replaces separate sales, stock and accounts spreadsheets with an ERP plus CRM. Sales staff must enter orders in one form; warehouse staff see reservations immediately; managers review one stock report. The gain comes only after staff are trained and old spreadsheets are retired.

keyPoints: ERP integrates core transactions, CRM manages customer relationships, and SCM coordinates suppliers and deliveries.
Integration shares master data and triggers processes, often through middleware.
ERP difficulties commonly arise from process, data and change issues, not only software faults.
Vendor selection should compare process fit, total cost, support, references and integration options.
Phased rollouts and strong data governance reduce implementation risk.
Organisational change needs sponsorship, training, communication and retirement of old systems.

en.title: Project management for information systems
en.short: Scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and stakeholders, plus waterfall, agile, WBS and critical path.

sections.heading: Six areas
sections.text: Project management for information systems is the planning and control of work so that a system is delivered within agreed scope, time, cost and quality. Scope management defines what the project will and will not include. Schedule management sets activity dates and dependencies. Cost management estimates and controls the budget. Quality management checks fitness for purpose and agreed standards. Risk management identifies uncertain events and plans responses. Stakeholder management identifies people affected and keeps their expectations realistic. These areas compete: adding scope usually raises cost and time.

sections.heading: Waterfall and agile
sections.text: Waterfall runs phases in sequence: requirements, design, build, test and deployment. It fixes scope early, documents each stage and suits stable requirements or strict contracts. Agile delivers small increments, keeps a prioritised backlog and reviews working software with users often. It suits uncertain requirements but needs customer involvement and disciplined testing. Many projects use hybrids.

sections.heading: Work breakdown
sections.text: A work breakdown structure (WBS) splits the project into deliverables and work packages. Each package can be estimated for cost and duration and assigned an owner. The WBS is the base for the schedule, budget and responsibility matrix. For example, a student records system might split into admissions, results and reporting, each with design, build and test packages.

sections.heading: Critical path
sections.text: Critical path scheduling finds the longest chain of dependent activities. That chain sets the shortest possible project duration, and its activities have zero slack. Example: A takes 3 days; B after A takes 4; C after A takes 2; D after B and C takes 5; E after D takes 3. Paths are A-B-D-E = 3+4+5+3 = 15 days and A-C-D-E = 3+2+5+3 = 13 days. The critical path is A-B-D-E at 15 days; C has 2 days of slack.

keyPoints: Scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and stakeholder management must be balanced because changing one affects the others.
Waterfall fixes scope early and suits stable requirements; agile uses short increments and suits changing requirements.
A WBS decomposes deliverables into work packages for estimating and assigning responsibility.
The critical path is the longest dependent path; it sets the minimum project duration and has zero slack.
Slack = latest start − earliest start, or latest finish − earliest finish.
Update estimates, schedules and risk plans as the project proceeds.

en.title: Information systems strategy and governance
en.short: Aligning IS with goals, appraising investment, sourcing choices and IT governance.

sections.heading: Strategic alignment
sections.text: Strategic alignment means fitting information systems plans to organisational goals, not buying technology for its own sake. It asks which capabilities create value, which risks matter and how spending supports priorities. A practical test is traceability: each major proposal should name the goal, process, owner and success measure. Alignment is continuous. A distributor wanting faster order fulfilment may gain more from stock visibility than from a new website.

sections.heading: Investment appraisal
sections.text: Investment appraisal compares costs and benefits. Payback is the time to recover the outlay. Net present value (NPV) discounts future cash flows at a required rate and subtracts the initial cost; positive NPV adds value. Return on investment is profit divided by cost. Total cost of ownership includes purchase, operation, support and exit costs. Intangible benefits need explicit assumptions. Example: a system costs 100,000 and yields 30,000 a year for five years, cash flows at year end, discount rate 10%. Payback = 100,000 ÷ 30,000 = 3.33 years. The five-year annuity factor is 3.7908, so NPV = −100,000 + 30,000 × 3.7908 = 13,724, which is positive.

sections.heading: Sourcing decisions
sections.text: Sourcing decides who provides systems and services. Options include build in house, buy a package, outsource, offshore or use cloud services. Compare them on total cost, fit, speed, skills, control, data protection and exit risk. Outsourcing can cut cost or add capability, but it needs clear service level agreements (SLAs), performance measures and exit terms. Vendor lock-in and lost internal knowledge are risks. Keep core, differentiating capabilities under close control.

sections.heading: IT governance
sections.text: IT governance is the decision rights and accountabilities that direct and control IT. It answers who decides, who is accountable and how performance is monitored. ISO/IEC 38500 sets principles for corporate governance of IT. COBIT provides governance and management objectives. ITIL is widely used for service management. The board sets strategy, risk appetite and oversight; the audit committee checks controls; the CIO and IT managers execute and report. Governance separates approval, delivery and assurance.

keyPoints: Strategic alignment links each IS proposal to a named organisational goal, owner and success measure.
Payback = initial outlay ÷ annual net cash inflow.
NPV = −initial cost + Σ cash flow ÷ (1 + r)^t; positive NPV adds value at the chosen rate.
Sourcing choices compare total cost of ownership, fit, risk, control and exit terms, not just price.
IT governance assigns decision rights and accountability for IT.
Boards set IT strategy and risk appetite, while IT management executes and reports, and assurance checks controls.

en.title: E-commerce and digital business
en.short: E-commerce models, payments, digital marketing, platforms, trust and consumer law.

sections.heading: Business models
sections.text: E-commerce is buying and selling goods or services over the internet. Digital business is wider: it uses digital technology to create value and reach customers. A business model explains the customer, the value offered and how money is made. Common models are business to consumer (B2C), business to business (B2B) and consumer to consumer (C2C). Revenue may come from sales, subscriptions, commissions, advertising or freemium, where basic use is free and extras are paid for.

sections.heading: Payments and trust
sections.text:
An online payment needs a payment gateway, which passes card or mobile money details to a bank or payment provider. Mobile money is common where card use is low. Escrow holds the buyer’s money until delivery, and a chargeback reverses a card payment after a dispute. Trust depends on clear prices, delivery terms, privacy notices, verified reviews and complaint handling.

Case: Amina sells shea butter on a marketplace that holds payment in escrow until delivery and shows verified reviews. Buyers trust it more, and disputes are recorded.

sections.heading: Marketing and platforms
sections.text: Digital marketing uses search engine optimisation (SEO), content, social media, email, paid search and affiliate links. It is measurable: analytics show clicks, conversion rate and customer acquisition cost. Consent matters for email and tracking. A platform-based business is a multi-sided market that brings groups together. It grows through network effects: each new user makes the platform more useful to others. Platforms face the chicken-and-egg problem, so they often subsidise one side and earn from commissions, fees or advertising.

sections.heading: Law and protection
sections.text: Consumer protection covers fair advertising, clear contract terms, data protection, secure payment and redress. Rules differ by country and change often. In Nigeria, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 created the FCCPC, and the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 regulates personal data. The EU has the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Sellers must check the law where they and their customers are based, including tax, electronic signatures and distance selling. This is general information, not legal advice.

keyPoints: An e-commerce business model states the customer, the value offered and how revenue is earned.
Payment gateways, mobile money, escrow and chargeback rules shape online payment risk.
Digital marketing is measurable through conversion rate and customer acquisition cost, and consent is needed for tracking and email.
Platforms are multi-sided markets that grow through network effects and must solve the chicken-and-egg problem.
Trust is built with clear terms, secure payment, verified reviews and fair dispute handling.
Consumer, data protection and distance-selling laws vary by country, so check the current official rules.

en.title: Business intelligence and analytics
en.short: OLAP, KPIs, dashboards and descriptive analytics for management reporting and decision support.

sections.heading: From operations to reporting
sections.text: Operational systems record day-to-day transactions: sales, stock, payments. For management reporting, these data are extracted, cleaned and loaded into a data warehouse or data mart, often on a schedule. A data mart is a smaller warehouse for one department or subject. Cleaning removes duplicates and fixes inconsistent codes. The BI layer then queries the prepared data and presents reports, charts and dashboards. Data quality and timeliness matter: a report is only useful if managers trust it and it arrives in time to act.

sections.heading: OLAP
sections.text: OLAP means online analytical processing. Data is arranged as a cube: measures are numbers to analyse, such as sales revenue or units sold; dimensions are the ways to break them down, such as product, region, month and channel. Managers can slice (fix one dimension), dice (select values on two or more dimensions), drill down to detail, roll up to summary, and pivot to swap rows and columns. OLAP supports fast exploration of large summary data, not transaction entry.

sections.heading: KPIs and dashboards
sections.text: A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measure tied to an organisation’s goals, and organisations use only a small number of them. A good KPI is defined precisely, has an owner, a target and a time period, and is hard to manipulate. A dashboard displays current KPIs and trends on one screen, using charts, gauges and colour. Operational dashboards monitor daily activity; strategic dashboards track longer-term goals. Too many indicators hide the important ones.

sections.heading: Descriptive analytics
sections.text: Descriptive analytics summarises historical data to answer what happened and how much. It uses aggregation, trend lines, comparisons with target or previous period, and segmentation. Diagnostic analytics goes further, testing why a change occurred. Example: an online shop had 4,500 orders from 150,000 sessions this month, and 4,000 from 140,000 last month. Conversion rate = orders ÷ sessions × 100. This month: 4,500 ÷ 150,000 × 100 = 3.00%. Last month: 4,000 ÷ 140,000 × 100 = 2.86%. The rate rose by 0.14 percentage points, a relative rise of about 5%. The manager checks whether a campaign or site change caused it before acting.

keyPoints: Operational data is extracted, cleaned and loaded into a warehouse or data mart before BI reporting.
OLAP cubes organise data by measures and dimensions and support slice, dice, drill-down, roll-up and pivot.
A KPI is a precise, owned measure tied to a goal, with a target and time period.
Dashboards show current KPIs and trends on one screen; too many indicators reduce clarity.
Descriptive analytics summarises past data using aggregation, trends, comparisons and segmentation.
Conversion rate = orders ÷ sessions × 100; 4,500 ÷ 150,000 × 100 = 3.00%.

en.title: Data warehousing and data mining
en.short: Warehouse architecture, star schemas, ETL, classification and clustering, model evaluation and mining limits.

sections.heading: Warehouse architecture
sections.text: A data warehouse is a central store of integrated, subject-oriented, time-variant data built for analysis, not daily transactions. Its architecture has source systems, an ETL layer, a staging area, the warehouse and departmental data marts. Metadata records sources, transformations and definitions. Operational systems hold current records; the warehouse keeps history. Data marts are smaller subsets, dependent if fed from the warehouse or independent if built separately. Agree the grain (what one row represents) and the measures before loading.

sections.heading: Star schemas and ETL
sections.text: A star schema has one fact table at the centre and dimension tables around it. The fact table stores measures such as quantity and revenue plus foreign keys to dimensions such as date, product and store. The dimension tables are denormalised for simple queries. A snowflake schema normalises dimensions into sub-dimensions. ETL means extract, transform, load: extract from sources, clean and conform data by fixing duplicates, standardising codes and converting currencies, then load. Example: a retail chain maps product codes from two shops to one product key and stores revenue at the grain of one sale line.

sections.heading: Mining tasks
sections.text: Data mining finds patterns in large data. Classification is supervised: a model learns from labelled examples to predict a class, such as will repay or will default. Clustering is unsupervised: it groups similar records without labels, for customer segmentation. Other tasks include regression, association rules and anomaly detection. A model depends on its features and training data.

sections.heading: Evaluation and limits
sections.text: Evaluate classification on held-out data (holdout split or k-fold cross-validation). A confusion matrix counts true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN). Accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ (TP + FP + TN + FN). For TP = 40, FP = 10, TN = 45, FN = 5, accuracy = 85 ÷ 100 = 85%; precision = 40 ÷ 50 = 80%; recall = 40 ÷ 45 = 88.9%. Clustering is judged by cohesion and separation. Mining shows associations not causes. Poor data, overfitting, bias, privacy and spurious patterns limit results; validate with experts and fresh data.

keyPoints: Data warehouses store integrated, subject-oriented, time-variant data for analysis, fed by ETL from source systems.
Star schemas use one fact table of measures and keys linked to denormalised dimension tables.
ETL extracts, cleans and conforms data, then loads it at a defined grain.
Classification is supervised prediction; clustering is unsupervised grouping.
Evaluate classifiers on held-out data with a confusion matrix; accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ (TP + FP + TN + FN), precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP), recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN).
Mining finds patterns, not causes; poor data, overfitting, bias and privacy risks require expert and fresh-data validation.

en.title: Information security and risk management
en.short: CIA triad, threats and controls, risk assessment, incident response, continuity and legal duties.

sections.heading: CIA triad
sections.text: Information security protects information from harm. The CIA triad names three goals. Confidentiality means only authorised people can read data. Integrity means data is accurate and has not been changed without permission. Availability means systems and data are there when needed. A control is a safeguard that supports these goals. Controls can be technical, such as encryption or access control; administrative, such as policies and staff training; or physical, such as locks and guards.

sections.heading: Threats and controls
sections.text: Common threats include malware, phishing, denial of service, insider misuse and lost devices. A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat can exploit. Defence in depth uses several controls so one failure does not expose everything. Examples are strong authentication, patching, backups, network filtering and awareness training. No control removes all risk.

sections.heading: Risk assessment
sections.text:
Risk assessment identifies assets, threats and vulnerabilities, then estimates likelihood and impact. Qualitative scales are common. Quantitative risk uses money. Single loss expectancy (SLE) is the cost of one event. Annualised rate of occurrence (ARO) is expected events per year. Annualised loss expectancy (ALE) = SLE × ARO.
Example: SLE = 2,000,000 units of currency, ARO = 0.25, so ALE = 500,000 units. If a control costs 300,000 units a year, it is worth considering. Treatment options are avoid, reduce, transfer and accept.

sections.heading: Response and continuity
sections.text: Incident response has phases: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover and learn. Business continuity keeps essential services running. A business impact analysis sets recovery time objectives (RTO), the maximum acceptable downtime, and recovery point objectives (RPO), the maximum acceptable data loss. Backups and disaster recovery sites support these aims. Legal duties vary by country and sector. Data protection and breach notification laws may require prompt notice of breaches and can impose fines for breaking them. Check the current official source for your jurisdiction.

keyPoints: The CIA triad is confidentiality, integrity and availability.
A threat exploits a vulnerability; controls reduce risk but cannot remove it.
ALE = SLE × ARO estimates expected yearly loss.
Risk treatment options are avoid, reduce, transfer and accept.
Incident response phases are prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover and learn.
RTO limits downtime and RPO limits data loss; legal duties vary by country, so check current official rules.

en.title: IT infrastructure and cloud computing
en.short: Servers, storage, networks, virtualisation and data centres; cloud service and deployment models and adoption issues.

sections.heading: Building blocks
sections.text: A server is a computer that provides services to other computers. Storage keeps data persistently: block storage for disks, file storage for shared folders and object storage for large unstructured items. A network connects these components. A data centre houses servers, storage and network equipment with power, cooling and physical security. These parts are designed together because a weak link, such as a slow network, limits the whole system.

sections.heading: Virtualisation
sections.text: Virtualisation uses a hypervisor, a software layer, to divide one physical server into several virtual machines. Each virtual machine runs its own operating system and behaves like a separate computer. This raises utilisation and speeds provisioning. Containers are lighter: they share the host operating system kernel. Virtualisation lets cloud providers sell computing capacity in small units.

sections.heading: Cloud service models
sections.text: Cloud computing is on-demand access over a network to a shared pool of configurable resources. In Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) the provider supplies virtual machines, storage and networks; the customer manages the operating system and applications. In Platform as a Service (PaaS) the provider also supplies the runtime, database and tools, so the customer deploys code. In Software as a Service (SaaS) the provider runs the whole application, such as email, and the customer only uses it.

sections.heading: Deployment and management
sections.text: Deployment models are public (shared provider), private (one organisation), hybrid (a mix) and community (shared by organisations with common needs). Management issues include cost control under pay-as-you-go, service level agreements (SLAs), vendor lock-in, data location and data protection law, security under a shared responsibility model, latency and skills. A college in Kenya, with IT manager Amina, might run an exams portal on IaaS, use a managed database (PaaS) and email (SaaS), but keep student records private for legal reasons, so the design is hybrid. Amina must check the SLA, forecast cost and write an exit plan.

keyPoints: A data centre combines servers, storage, networks, power and cooling.
Virtualisation uses a hypervisor to share one physical server among virtual machines.
IaaS gives virtual infrastructure, PaaS gives a development platform, SaaS gives a finished application.
Deployment models are public, private, hybrid and community.
Cloud adoption needs control of cost, SLAs, lock-in, data location, security and exit.
Under shared responsibility the provider secures the cloud and the customer secures data and access.

en.title: Human-computer interaction and usability
en.short: User-centred design, usability heuristics, evaluation methods and accessibility in information systems.

sections.heading: User-centred design
sections.text:
Human-computer interaction (HCI) studies how people use computer systems. Usability is the extent to which specified users can achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use (ISO 9241-11).

User-centred design puts those users and their tasks first: study the work, prototype the interface, test it with real users, and repeat. It is not just making screens attractive; it is fitting the system to the task.

sections.heading: Heuristics and accessibility
sections.text:
Usability heuristics are broad rules of thumb. Nielsen’s ten include visibility of system status, match between system and real world, user control and freedom, consistency, error prevention, recognition rather than recall, and helpful error messages. They guide design and cheap expert review.

Accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, operate and understand the system. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), from the W3C, organise this as perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. Legal duties vary by country, so check local law.

sections.heading: Evaluation methods
sections.text:
Evaluation can be formative (during design) or summative (against targets). Heuristic evaluation has experts inspect the interface against heuristics. Usability testing observes representative users attempting realistic tasks, noting completion, errors and time. Cognitive walkthrough steps through a task from the user’s point of view.

Questionnaires such as the System Usability Scale measure perceived usability. Field studies and analytics show use in real work. Use more than one method; each catches different problems.

sections.heading: Design and adoption
sections.text:
Interface design affects adoption, productivity and satisfaction. A clinic stock system in Kano, used by Amina, may be accurate but rejected if the reorder screen hides expiry dates and needs many clicks.

Poor design raises errors and training time, lowering productivity; clear feedback and simple flows build trust and satisfaction. Good HCI therefore turns a technically working information system into one people actually use.

keyPoints: Usability means effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction for specified users, goals and context.
User-centred design repeats study, prototype and test with real users.
Heuristic evaluation uses experts and rules of thumb; usability testing uses representative users on realistic tasks.
Accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, operate and understand the system; WCAG principles are perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.
Poor interface design reduces adoption and productivity and raises errors, while good design builds satisfaction.
Use several evaluation methods because each finds different problems.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and law in information systems
en.short: Codes, ethical theories, privacy, intellectual property and computer misuse law for IS practice.

sections.heading: Codes and duties
sections.text: Codes of conduct are rules that professional bodies and employers publish. They set duties such as competence, honesty, confidentiality and avoiding conflicts of interest. Examples include the BCS Code of Conduct, the ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct, and the IEEE Code of Ethics. A code is not a statute; it guides judgement and may support disciplinary action. Some countries also have a statutory regulator, such as the Computer Professionals Registration Council of Nigeria (CPN).

sections.heading: Ethical reasoning
sections.text: Utilitarianism judges an action by its consequences, seeking the greatest overall benefit. Deontology judges by duties and rules, such as keeping promises and respecting persons. Virtue ethics asks what an honest, fair and prudent professional would do. Stakeholder analysis identifies everyone affected, including people who cannot speak for themselves. Case: Amina, a junior analyst at a Lagos bank, finds a report with customers’ account numbers. Her manager asks her to email it to a vendor. She checks policy, removes unnecessary data, and escalates the request. This applies duty, consequences and care.

sections.heading: Privacy and property
sections.text: Privacy is a person’s control over personal data. Data protection law requires lawful, fair and transparent processing, purpose limitation, data minimisation, security, and rights to access and correction. Laws differ: the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 and other national laws have different scope and penalties. Intellectual property protects creations. Copyright covers software code and text, patents cover inventions, trademarks cover signs, and trade secrets cover confidential information. Software licences set permitted use; open source licences rely on copyright. Check current national legislation and professional guidance.

sections.heading: Computer misuse
sections.text: Computer misuse laws criminalise unauthorised access, modification or interference with systems, and sometimes fraud or denial of service. Examples include the UK Computer Misuse Act 1990 and Nigeria’s Cybercrimes Act 2015. Names, offences and penalties vary by country. Do not test systems without written permission; report weaknesses responsibly and keep evidence. Consult the current statute, regulator and professional code.

keyPoints: Codes of conduct set professional duties but are not statutes; check the current code and any statutory regulator.
Utilitarianism, deontology and virtue ethics give different, sometimes conflicting, ways to judge an IS decision.
Privacy and data protection law require lawful, fair, minimal and transparent use of personal data, but rules differ by country.
Intellectual property includes copyright, patents, trademarks and trade secrets; software licences define permitted use.
Computer misuse laws punish unauthorised access or interference, and penalties vary by country.
Always consult current national legislation, regulator guidance and the relevant professional code before acting.

en.title: Emerging technologies and digital transformation
en.short: How digital transformation changes organisations, plus AI, IoT, blockchain, adoption and hype.

sections.heading: Transformation, not tools
sections.text:
Digitisation turns analogue records into digital form. Digitalisation uses digital technology to improve an existing process. Digital transformation is wider: an organisation changes its processes, capabilities, culture and sometimes its business model so that digital technology creates new value. It is a management and organisational change, not a software purchase.

A useful test is whether customers, staff or partners do something materially different. If a bank only scans its paper form into a computer file, that is digitisation. If it lets customers fill the form online, that is digitalisation. If it redesigns lending around data and fast decisions, that is transformation.

sections.heading: Three technologies
sections.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) covers systems that perform tasks such as classification, prediction or language generation. In organisations it can score loan applications or forecast demand, but it needs good data and human oversight.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical devices with sensors that send data. It supports remote monitoring, predictive maintenance and stock tracking.

Blockchain is a shared ledger copied across participants, where new entries can be added but old ones cannot be changed. It can record transactions without one central owner, which may help traceability and trust between organisations, but it is slow and costly for simple records.

sections.heading: Adoption and change
sections.text:
Adoption is the process by which people accept and use a new system. Change management is the planned work of preparing people: explaining the purpose, mapping new roles, training, listening to concerns and changing incentives. Pilots and feedback reduce risk.

Case: Ngozi runs a distributor in Lagos, Nigeria. She tests vehicle sensors, an AI late-delivery alert and a supplier ledger. The technology works, but drivers still use paper and suppliers distrust the ledger. Value appears only after Ngozi changes routines, trains staff and agrees shared rules.

sections.heading: Hype and value
sections.text: Hype is attention without evidence. Practical value depends on fit with the problem, total cost, skills, data quality, security, regulation and measurable outcomes. Ask for a small trial with baseline measures, not a demonstration. Many emerging technologies are useful in some settings and poor value in others.

keyPoints: Digital transformation is organisation-wide change in processes, capabilities, culture and value creation, not just buying technology.
AI supports classification and prediction but needs good data and human oversight.
IoT links sensor-equipped devices to monitor and automate physical operations.
Blockchain is a shared ledger that can support traceability but is not always worth its cost.
Adoption depends on change management: roles, training, incentives and shared rules.
Judge emerging technology by evidence of practical value, not by hype.

en.title: Information systems research methods and theory
en.short: Paradigms, theory building and testing, qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods, design and dissertation planning.

sections.heading: Paradigms and theory
sections.text: Paradigms are beliefs about reality (ontology) and knowledge (epistemology). Positivism assumes an objective reality that can be measured, so it favours hypotheses and statistics. Interpretivism assumes reality is socially constructed, so it favours meaning, context and interviews. Critical theory asks whose interests a system serves. Pragmatism judges methods by usefulness, supporting mixed methods. A theory is constructs and propositions that explain or predict a phenomenon. Theory building can be inductive (data to concepts) or deductive (theory to hypotheses). Theory testing operationalises constructs as measures, then checks reliability and validity.

sections.heading: Methods and designs
sections.text: Qualitative methods, such as interviews, case studies and ethnography, produce rich textual data and suit questions about meaning and process. Quantitative methods, such as surveys, experiments and secondary data analysis, produce numbers and suit questions about relationships and effects. Mixed methods combine both. Explanatory sequential design starts with quantitative results and uses qualitative work to explain them; exploratory sequential design starts with qualitative work to build a survey or model. The choice must fit the research question. Sampling, analysis and ethics are planned together.

sections.heading: Review and design
sections.text: A literature review is not a list of summaries. It uses a search strategy, appraises sources and synthesises them to show what is known and where the gap is. Systematic reviews state inclusion criteria and are reproducible; narrative reviews are broader. Research design links the question, paradigm, method, sampling, data collection, analysis and quality criteria. For qualitative work, trustworthiness covers credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability. For quantitative work, validity, reliability and generalisability matter.

sections.heading: Dissertation planning
sections.text: Dissertation planning turns the design into a feasible proposal: a clear question, a clear literature gap, an ethics approval plan, a timeline, and a data management plan. A useful case: an MSc student in Lagos studies why market traders adopt mobile money. She uses pragmatism, interviews traders to build a model, then surveys a sample to test it. She keeps a pilot, a coding frame and a reflective log.

keyPoints: Paradigms differ in their ontology and epistemology, and the choice must fit the research question.
Theory building moves from constructs to propositions; theory testing turns constructs into measures and checks reliability and validity.
Qualitative methods suit meaning and process, quantitative methods suit relationships and effects, and mixed methods combine both.
A literature review must synthesise sources and identify a gap, not just summarise them.
Research design aligns question, paradigm, method, sampling, analysis, ethics and quality criteria.
Dissertation planning should show feasibility through a proposal, timeline, ethics plan and data management plan.

en.title: Advanced data analytics and machine learning
en.short: Supervised and unsupervised learning, text analytics, evaluation, deployment, bias and ethics.

sections.heading: Learning paradigms
sections.text: Supervised learning uses labelled examples to learn a mapping from inputs to outputs. Classification predicts a category, such as fraud or not fraud; regression predicts a number, such as demand. Unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data to find structure. Clustering groups similar records; dimensionality reduction compresses many variables into fewer components while keeping useful variation. A model trained on past data assumes the future resembles the past, so domain knowledge and data quality matter.

sections.heading: Text and evaluation
sections.text: Text analytics turns unstructured text into features. Bag of words counts terms; TF-IDF downweights common terms and upweights distinctive ones; embeddings represent meaning as vectors. Models are evaluated on data held back from training, using a test set or cross-validation. A confusion matrix gives true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. With 18 true positives, 6 false positives, 12 false negatives and 64 true negatives: accuracy = (18+64) ÷ 100 = 0.82; precision = 18 ÷ (18+6) = 0.75; recall = 18 ÷ (18+12) = 0.60; F1 = 2 × 0.75 × 0.60 ÷ (0.75+0.60) = 0.67. Accuracy alone can mislead when classes are imbalanced.

sections.heading: Deployment and governance
sections.text: Deployment puts a model into organisational work: batch scoring, an API, or a decision-support screen. It needs versioning, monitoring for data drift, retraining rules, access control and an owner. Governance defines who may use the output and for what decision. A model is not a policy; staff need training and a route to challenge errors.

sections.heading: Bias and ethics
sections.text: Bias enters through sampling, labels, proxies and past decisions. Interpretability means people can understand why a model produced an output; simple models help, and post-hoc explanations can help but may be incomplete. Ethical analytics requires lawful basis, consent where required, privacy, fairness testing, transparency and accountability.
