Rules differ by country, so check the current data protection and sector rules. Keep a human decision-maker accountable for high-impact choices.

keyPoints: Supervised learning uses labelled data; unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data.
Text analytics converts text into numeric features such as bag-of-words, TF-IDF or embeddings.
Evaluate models on held-back data with precision, recall and F1, not accuracy alone.
Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP); recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN); F1 = 2 × precision × recall ÷ (precision + recall).
Deployment requires monitoring, versioning, retraining rules and clear ownership.
Bias, interpretability, privacy, fairness and accountability must be governed, with human oversight for high-impact decisions.

en.title: Digital platforms and transformation strategy
en.short: Platform models, network effects, ecosystems, governance, competition and organisational change.

sections.heading: Platform models
sections.text:
A digital platform creates value by enabling interactions between two or more groups. A multi-sided platform is a matchmaker: it reduces search and transaction costs and earns from fees, subscriptions, advertising or data services. Marketplaces, app stores and payment networks are examples.

The platform governs access and rules rather than owning most of the assets that create value. A pipeline business makes and sells a product step by step. Strategy shifts from controlling a value chain to orchestrating an ecosystem of users and complementors, firms that add products or services.

sections.heading: Network effects and ecosystems
sections.text:
Network effects exist when each additional user raises value for others. Direct effects occur within one group. Indirect or cross-side effects occur between groups: more drivers make a ride-hailing app better for riders, and more riders attract drivers. Strong effects can produce tipping, where the market shifts quickly toward one platform, and winner-take-most markets, but multi-homing, using several platforms at once, weakens this.

An ecosystem is the platform plus complementors and partners linked by APIs (application programming interfaces) and standards. Governance decides who may join, what they may do, how revenue and data are shared, and how disputes are settled.

sections.heading: Transformation strategy
sections.text:
Digital transformation strategy is the coordinated redesign of strategy, operating model, technology and capabilities. It is not one IT project. A platform strategy asks which interactions to enable, which side to subsidise to solve the chicken-and-egg problem, how open to be, and how to monetise.

Example: Ada starts a Lagos freight platform. Shippers will not join without carriers, so she recruits carriers first with free onboarding and charges shippers a commission. She measures match rate and repeat use, not registrations.

sections.heading: Governance and change
sections.text:
Platform governance balances openness and control. Too open invites poor quality and fraud; too closed discourages complementors. Competition authorities in several jurisdictions, including the European Union, examine self-preferencing, fees and data access; rules differ by country, so check local law.

Organisations moving to platforms need product teams, platform teams, skills, revised incentives and leadership support. Change is socio-technical: roles, processes and culture change together.

keyPoints: A multi-sided platform creates value by matching groups and governing their interactions.
Direct network effects operate within one user group; cross-side effects operate between groups.
Strong network effects can cause tipping, but multi-homing can reduce winner-take-most outcomes.
Platform ecosystems depend on complementors and on governance rules for access, data and revenue.
Digital transformation strategy coordinates technology, operating model and capabilities, not just an IT project.
Organisational change in platform settings requires product and platform teams, new skills and revised incentives.

en.title: Socio-technical design and AI ethics
en.short: Socio-technical systems, participatory design, automation effects, AI ethics and accountable responsible systems.

sections.heading: Socio-technical systems
sections.text: Socio-technical systems theory treats an information system as two linked subsystems: the social (people, roles, skills, culture, incentives) and the technical (software, data, processes, infrastructure). Joint optimisation means designing both together, because a change in one produces ripple effects in the other. Work is emergent: people adapt tools and routines, so outcomes cannot be read off the software alone. A hospital records system may be technically correct yet fail if ward staff lack time or trust to enter data.

sections.heading: Participatory design
sections.text: Participatory design makes users and other stakeholders co-designers, not just sources of requirements. It comes from Scandinavian workplace democracy projects and suits settings where work is skilled and context matters. Done well, it improves fit, surfaces tacit knowledge and builds ownership. Done badly, it becomes token consultation or lets the loudest group dominate. In a Lagos microfinance bank, Ngozi the loan officer and applicant representatives join workshops before an AI screening tool is configured, so thin credit histories and appeal routes are discussed early.

sections.heading: Automation and AI at work
sections.text: Automation usually replaces or reshapes tasks rather than whole jobs. It can raise speed and consistency, but it can also narrow discretion, increase monitoring and create new shadow work such as correcting errors. Algorithmic management assigns, rates or disciplines workers through data. The future of work is best analysed task by task: which tasks are substituted, which are augmented, and who gains the new skills. Power and job quality matter as much as productivity.

sections.heading: Responsible AI and accountability
sections.text: AI ethics covers fairness, transparency, privacy, safety, human oversight and contestability (the ability to challenge a decision). Accountability means a named person or body can answer for the system and provide redress. Responsibility gaps appear when no single actor has enough control or knowledge to answer for outcomes, so responsibility is diffused or passed between developers, vendors and managers. Responsible information systems use impact assessments, participation, audit logs, human review and monitoring after deployment. The microfinance tool should have an owner, monthly bias checks and a clear appeal path.

keyPoints: Socio-technical design optimises social and technical subsystems together.
Participatory design treats users as co-designers and needs real influence, not token consultation.
Automation changes tasks, skills, discretion and monitoring, not just headcount.
AI ethics includes fairness, transparency, privacy, safety, human oversight and contestability.
Accountability requires a named owner, audit trails and a route to redress.
Responsible systems are monitored after deployment and can be challenged.
